title: Working in Extended Reality
summary: Doug Bowman, Professor of Computer Science at Virginia Tech, joins Kyle to explore how augmented reality, virtual reality, and AI are reshaping the future of human-computer interaction. title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
summary: Sam Herring ’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves? He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro work, and the loop Nous is building around it: find the exact point where an agent fails, cluster those failures by type, synthesize environments that recreate them, and train on them again and again. The second half moves from training to inference. We get into whether reasoning models overthink, why leaning on pretraining knowledge can be a model’s Achilles heel, and why choosing a reasoning effort level may be a temporary quirk. Sam also makes his case for activation steering as an underexplored way to get more out of small models, explains where steering meets interpretability, and describes what true continual learning could look like. title: Getting Pharma AI Agents to the Right Answer by Fixing the Data and Semantic Layers - with Richard Knoche of Flatiron Health
summary: Pharma is moving toward AI agents, but agents only know the context they are given, so gaps in data and meaning turn into wrong answers at scale. In this episode, Richard Knoche, Head of Data Science and AI at Flatiron Health, explains why a strong data foundation and a well-built semantic layer determine whether AI agents can be trusted with complex real-world data. He walks through how historical human analyses can be used to build and benchmark that semantic layer, why having agents resolve ambiguity before answering improves accuracy and reduces handoffs between teams, and why leaders need centralized data governance and agents that plug into any system rather than siloed, bespoke tools. ​ This episode is sponsored by Flatiron Health ​ Emerj works with a select group of AI vendors to reach Fortune 500 decision makers through research, media, and direct access. title: Interview #100 Peter Evans, CEO at Xtract One Technologies
summary: Peter Evans, CEO at Xtract One Technologies, breaks down why many AI weapons scanners at school and stadium entrances still measure the wrong things. He explains why most "AI-enabled" detectors rest on the same physics as a walk-through metal detector, why knives and laptops expose the limits of that physics, and why a claim of 3,000 people an hour means little if a weak model sends most of them to a bag check. Peter also dives into how to estimate the weapons a system misses when nobody reports them, who should own the sensitivity dial, and what should have happened before police drew weapons on a teenager after a Maryland AI camera mistook a bag of chips for a gun. Finally, he shares why mandates in California and Georgia are racing ahead of testing standards, what an entrance should never be allowed to know about you, and why a 3D printed gun is still not invisible. title: Why AI Goes Rogue: Turing Award Winner Explains Reward Failure | Andrew Barto
summary: Andrew Barto on Rewards Gone Rogue Andrew Barto helped found reinforcement learning. He and Richard Sutton wrote the field's standard textbook, and they shared the Turing Award for that work. Reinforcement learning now trains today's reasoning models and AI agents. It also sits behind some of their strangest behavior, including the recent cases of agents breaking out of their sandboxes. Craig visited Barto at his home on Cape Cod. They talked about where rewards come from and why they are so hard to get right. Barto traces the problem back to Norbert Wiener's warnings in the 1950s. He explains how the dopamine system in the brain mirrors the learning algorithm he and Sutton developed. And he admits a weakness in their own framework: boiling every goal down to a single number. He also makes the case for engineering discipline. Ship designers learned their codes from wrecks and drowned sailors. Barto hopes AI can learn its lessons without that kind of cost. Subscribe to Eye on A.I. for weekly conversations with the people building and deploying the future of AI.

title: Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
summary: What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? Ioannis Zempekakis , Director of AI at Prosus , has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark. Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. The cheapest wins come from controlling context and running a basic model router, while ten new features a month keep sprouting like Hydra heads. From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. Ioannis explains how owning the stack let Prosus grow a GPT-3 Slack bot into a full agent harness. He also explains why committing to a single vendor or open source project is a bigger bet than it looks, and how to balance top-down priorities with bottom-up building across the company. We close on hiring. Ioannis looks for system design over syntax, a nose for the over-engineered code AI models love to produce, and enough agent intuition to know when to build something yourself and when to let the agent decide. title: Your Agent Ran One Command. It Did a Dozen Things.
summary: Chetan Conikee on Tracking Agent Behavior, Reducing Costs, and Preventing Security Incidents. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . Ben Lorica talks with Chetan Conikee , founder of Modiqo and creator of Olki , about why existing tools often fall short when it comes to understanding what AI agents actually do. Chetan explains how Olki captures and classifies individual agent actions without relying on another LLM, providing detailed insights into costs, performance, and security. They also discuss strategies for reducing token consumption, optimizing context compaction, detecting risky agent behavior, and the advantages of a local-first approach to monitoring agents. Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter Interview highlights – key sections from the video version: Introduction: Chetan Conikee, Modiqo, and Olki Why AI Agents Need Better Cost, Performance, and Security Monitoring Why Existing Agent Observability Tools Fall Short Operational Traces: What Traditional Monitoring Tools Miss Using Strict Type Systems Instead of LLMs to Classify Agent Actions Formal Verification and the Challenge of Accurately Capturing Agent Behavior Why Olki Avoids Using LLMs to Monitor Other LLMs Breaking Complex Agent Commands into Individual Operations Dashboards, Cost Attribution, and Measuring Agent Effectiveness Agent Security: Detecting Risky Actions and Preventing Log Tampering Why Local-First Monitoring Matters for Privacy and Enterprise Oversight Measuring Agent Outcomes and Tracing the Sources of AI Costs OpenTelemetry vs. Hooks: Capturing Agent Activity in Real Time Early User Feedback: Optimizing Context Compaction and Token Costs Security Controls, Shadow Mode, and the Roadmap for Olki Jump to transcript Related content : A video version of this conversation is available on our YouTube channel . Chetan Conikee at the AI Conference : Your agents’ traces are your most valuable asset: reading the software factory floor Nine Practical Rules for Agents Doing Real Work Eight Security Assumptions AI Agents Quietly Break Passing Your Evals Doesn’t Mean You’re Safe Abi Aryan → Your AI Agent Is Costing You More Than You Think Helen Gu → The Hidden Failure Modes of AI Agents Zhou Yu → Why Your AI Agent Isn’t Ready to Ship (And How to Know When It Is) Andrew Burt → Your AI Safety Tests Are Lying to You Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter Transcript Below is a polished and edited transcript . Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have my old friend Chetan Conikee, founder of Modiqo, which you can find at modiqo.ai. That’s M-O-D-I-Q-O dot AI. But more importantly for this episode, he is the creator of Olki, which you can find at olki.ai, and the tagline for Olki is “cost and type effects for agents.” So, Chetan, welcome to the podcast. Chetan Conikee. Thank you, Ben. Always a pleasure to talk to you. Ben Lorica. And full disclosure, I am an advisor to Modiqo and therefore Olki. But I will try my best to represent the audience in this discussion. First of all, the reason I wanted to talk to you about Olki is that I noticed your talk at AI Conference was quite popular. I wanted to understand what Olki is exactly, since I missed your talk. So first of all, Chetan, I guess a problem statement: What problem is Olki trying to address? Chetan Conikee. Thank you, Ben. For the most part, today I’m assuming all of us are using agents for everything. Particularly, I want to focus on those who are creators, because all of us are creating code that becomes applications, and much of that is going through an agent harness. The issue that we face as individuals or employees of an organization is that when we leverage these harnesses and inference providers, we are burning tokens. Meaning, we ask something, then that something becomes a long-running job, and as a consequence, we hit our limits, and those limits translate to dollars. The other thing is, when we create applications and code, we want to measure the efficiency of what is created. Because if we are spending money, we want to make sure that we create something meaningful and put it out there for others to use. And assume we don’t create anything meaningful. Lots of money gets wasted, and lots of time gets wasted, because we’re in the era of vibe coding. So it’s critical for us to have a pulse on this. Are we doing something useful? And if so, how do we measure that something useful? And finally—yeah, go ahead. Ben Lorica. Go ahead, go ahead. Chetan Conikee. And finally, we just ask the agent to do things, and we don’t have an idea of what the agent is doing. So, did you hint earlier that you already have some external teams using Olki? And if yes, what are some of the initial stories or feedback? Chetan Conikee. We have a couple of teams using Olki at this point, and each of these larger companies is operating in different domains. Some of the domains are inference providers. Some are designing newer chipsets and HBMs for the new AI ecosystem. Some are essentially running critical operations like finance and HR. So we are slowly distributing and diffusing our product to understand how to serve their needs. And eventually, if we start observing that they like what they see and they use it on a daily basis, we’re going to figure out a wider distribution of the same product. Ben Lorica. But are there some early users who have already gone back to you with stories of how Olki has changed how they do things? Chetan Conikee. Absolutely. The best feedback we received was from a company that said, “Okay, you give me all these insights, but I’m a human, and I’m as slow as my actions, right? Am I able to take those insights and enforce them?” For example, someone uses a harness, and the harness has to deal with something called compaction because it builds a prefix cache. And that prefix cache is how it optimally utilizes the relationship with the inference provider and has signals of what it needs to do. If you run the default harness, you keep hitting the one-million-token limit and compacting, right? And if you run it for 12 hours, you’ll notice a sawtooth graph of many, many compaction cycles. The side effect of this is your performance gets impacted, and you end up paying a lot of dollars for running that long-horizon agent. So I received feedback saying, “Hey, what if maybe we hit about five compaction cycles, and you’re able to use your own data in Olki and auto-compact?” So you influence the harness to auto-compact at maybe 250K, maybe 800K. With that, suddenly it becomes a dynamic system. It’s dynamic because it observes its own performance, behavior, and cost, and then auto-configures the system to a lower compaction threshold. Then it looks at errors because of lower compaction. It increases the threshold, so it becomes like a scheduler. It observes itself, orients itself. So we actually released it for them, and it’s working really well, both for us and for them. There’s a lot to learn, but at least across two harnesses, we are seeing the dividends pay back. Ben Lorica. So is there an argument, Chetan, that you can even assist the compaction because you have so much information? You can say, “Hey, not only should you do compaction now, but here are some key things that you should make sure you include in the compaction.” Chetan Conikee. Exactly. To your point, Ben, once you have fidelity of information, you can observe these amazing things. I’ll give you three quick examples. Example one is, if you leave the default configuration, it is a benefit to the harness provider—sorry, the inference provider—and a detriment to you. It’s a detriment because you start compounding costs, and over time, the accuracy of your harness loop reduces. The second is, all of us run agents continuously, but we take a couple of coffee breaks and bathroom breaks. And sometimes the harness wants to elicit information from you. So it’ll ask, “Hey Ben, I’m stuck. I need this particular advice from you before I proceed.” And if you don’t answer in a timely fashion, the cache on the harness side is also time-limited. So if the cache evicts and becomes cold, then all that data again has to build the stateful relationship between the harness and the inference provider. When we built Olki, we saw all of that. We saw that granularity of where the problems lie. So we actually built a ping system where, suppose you get interrupted and don’t answer, Olki keeps pinging that stateful server. That way, the cache stays warm, and it’s just a few kilobyte pings. And then when you come back, you still stick to that node in the inference provider. Ben Lorica. So you talked a lot about cost and FinOps. Now, in a previous life, you spent quite a bit of time with security people. So have you tried to explore that space in the context of Olki, in terms of reaching out to your contacts in the security space? I imagine they would love a tool like this, right? Chetan Conikee. I’m trying to position it in a way where it wows them when they use it, right? That’s when the unlock happens. And by the way, Olki saved me from a couple of incidents because when I hook up a commodity router for an LLM, sometimes it reaches out to a tool that I didn’t permit. I get information at the network level saying, “This particular URL was attempted. Do you approve or deny?” So there is huge opportunity for security to unlock. And the way I want to position it is, run it in shadow mode, observe for a week, and then start creating your policies to block. And it should come naturally. That’s what I’m hoping, where they first install it, then unlock each of these outcomes: the cost outcome, the performance outcome, the accuracy outcome, and the security outcome. Ben Lorica. All right. So looking ahead, over the next six to 12 months, obviously local-first is done. I’m assuming the enterprise offering is in the works. So what else is on the roadmap for the next six to 12 months for Olki? Chetan Conikee. This product came about serendipitously because we have a primary product. We’ll still be putting a lot of muscle into taking the primary product to market. I am testing the efficiency and the pull of this product by selectively demoing it, selectively enabling it. But as we see more need, more adoption, we are going to diffuse it and then start thinking about enterprise viability controls, the ability to run within sandboxes, outside sandboxes, etc. So the enterprise landscape is still open out there, which we should figure out as we progress. Ben Lorica. And like I mentioned, you gave a talk at AI Conference, which I will link to in the episode notes. But what was the feedback there? Chetan Conikee. Very good. I got lots of pingbacks from different industries. Lots of services companies pinged back. By services, I mean what they call managed service providers. These are the folks who run companies where they install harnesses, hook them up to inference, and set up your companies to be successful. They love this view because now they can remotely control how a harness operates and make it viable for cost, viable for performance. And that’s how they can become viable consultants. They can stay there and provide you value. I got a pingback from a few of them. I got pingbacks from a couple of Fortune 500s. So I’m actively conversing with them to unlock and provide them value in their target domains. Ben Lorica. And with that, thank you, Chetan. Chetan Conikee. Thank you, Ben. Always a pleasure. Appreciate it.
summary_html:
Chetan Conikee on Tracking Agent Behavior, Reducing Costs, and Preventing Security Incidents.


Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube •  AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon •  RSS.

Ben Lorica talks with Chetan Conikee, founder of Modiqo and creator of Olki, about why existing tools often fall short when it comes to understanding what AI agents actually do. Chetan explains how Olki captures and classifies individual agent actions without relying on another LLM, providing detailed insights into costs, performance, and security. They also discuss strategies for reducing token consumption, optimizing context compaction, detecting risky agent behavior, and the advantages of a local-first approach to monitoring agents.

Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter

Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:

      1. Introduction: Chetan Conikee, Modiqo, and Olki
      2. Why AI Agents Need Better Cost, Performance, and Security Monitoring
      3. Why Existing Agent Observability Tools Fall Short
      4. Operational Traces: What Traditional Monitoring Tools Miss
      5. Using Strict Type Systems Instead of LLMs to Classify Agent Actions
      6. Formal Verification and the Challenge of Accurately Capturing Agent Behavior
      7. Why Olki Avoids Using LLMs to Monitor Other LLMs
      8. Breaking Complex Agent Commands into Individual Operations
      9. Dashboards, Cost Attribution, and Measuring Agent Effectiveness
      10. Agent Security: Detecting Risky Actions and Preventing Log Tampering
      11. Why Local-First Monitoring Matters for Privacy and Enterprise Oversight
      12. Measuring Agent Outcomes and Tracing the Sources of AI Costs
      13. OpenTelemetry vs. Hooks: Capturing Agent Activity in Real Time
      14. Early User Feedback: Optimizing Context Compaction and Token Costs
      15. Security Controls, Shadow Mode, and the Roadmap for Olki

Transcript

Below is a polished and edited transcript.

Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have my old friend Chetan Conikee, founder of Modiqo, which you can find at modiqo.ai. That’s M-O-D-I-Q-O dot AI. But more importantly for this episode, he is the creator of Olki, which you can find at olki.ai, and the tagline for Olki is “cost and type effects for agents.” So, Chetan, welcome to the podcast.

Chetan Conikee. Thank you, Ben. Always a pleasure to talk to you.

Ben Lorica. And full disclosure, I am an advisor to Modiqo and therefore Olki. But I will try my best to represent the audience in this discussion. First of all, the reason I wanted to talk to you about Olki is that I noticed your talk at AI Conference was quite popular. I wanted to understand what Olki is exactly, since I missed your talk. So first of all, Chetan, I guess a problem statement: What problem is Olki trying to address?

Chetan Conikee. Thank you, Ben. For the most part, today I’m assuming all of us are using agents for everything. Particularly, I want to focus on those who are creators, because all of us are creating code that becomes applications, and much of that is going through an agent harness.

The issue that we face as individuals or employees of an organization is that when we leverage these harnesses and inference providers, we are burning tokens. Meaning, we ask something, then that something becomes a long-running job, and as a consequence, we hit our limits, and those limits translate to dollars.

The other thing is, when we create applications and code, we want to measure the efficiency of what is created. Because if we are spending money, we want to make sure that we create something meaningful and put it out there for others to use. And assume we don’t create anything meaningful. Lots of money gets wasted, and lots of time gets wasted, because we’re in the era of vibe coding.

So it’s critical for us to have a pulse on this. Are we doing something useful? And if so, how do we measure that something useful? And finally—yeah, go ahead.

Ben Lorica. Go ahead, go ahead.

Chetan Conikee. And finally, we just ask the agent to do things, and we don’t have an idea of what the agent is doing. To illustrate with a few examples, sometimes if you’re vague in your asking, the agent can delete your database, your folder, or perhaps exfiltrate some information if you’re connecting to some suspicious tool through OpenRouter or other ecosystems.

So, net-net, agents produce traces. Traces become information that can yield all these insights. Meaning, where are you spending? What is the agent doing? Is it secure or not?

Ben Lorica. All right. So everything you said, I completely buy, and that’s not because I’m your friend and advisor. Everything you’ve said makes sense.

On the other hand, I’m assuming there are existing tools, right? There are already tools that hook into coding agents and harnesses. There are tools that are basically runtimes at the OS level, that watch everything you’re doing on your computer and record it. And then there are tools built around OpenTelemetry and things like this.

So I’m assuming, since you were busy doing other things like Rote, that your first choice was not to build Olki, right? You were interested in everything you mentioned—efficiency, costs, effects, and all of these things—and there are tools out there. So what were the shortcomings of these tools?

Chetan Conikee. That’s a good question, Ben. To your point, we did not build Olki because we wanted to vibe-code something. That was not the motivation or impetus.

Ben Lorica. And also, to our listeners, you folks were busy building another thing called Rote, right?

Chetan Conikee. Exactly. Rote is our primary product, and what Rote does is observe agent behavior, capture that as traces, and convert those traces into workflows that can be repeated on a schedule. Think of it as operational memory for agents.

That was our motivation. But of course, like all of us who are building products in the world of agents, we have to make sure a product works uniformly across all these harnesses. You’ve got Claude Code, Codex, the Claude Code app, Hermes, OpenCode. There’s never an end to the number of harnesses being built today.

If we want to be successful with our product, we have to make sure it works uniformly across all these harnesses. Hence, we built an eval system to workbench and benchmark our solution, which is a CLI, and its efficiency across these harnesses.

So we started looking around. Firstly, we wanted to ensure that our product was working efficiently, and we needed a lens for that. The other is efficiency in terms of latency, meaning, is our product taking too long on agent execution?

There are many products in the observability space. Some of them use hooks. Some of them use OTel, or what they call OpenTelemetry. But we experienced lots of shortcomings because most of these observability tools work very naively.

By that I mean, if you look at any agent harness today, they don’t think command by command. If you say, “Read my repository, get the latest, get info, and then report to me,” it is going to execute one single command, which is piped, where you have cat piped to sed, which is for search, piped to awk, piped to something else, right?

If you look at all these observability systems, they just say, “Bash tool executed.” That’s it. And they give me this whole dump of large piped operations.

If you switch and use a frontier model like Astra or Claude Fable, they think in code most of the time, where if you ask a question, they’ll generate code to combine all the operations needed to get your response and provide that response.

Ben Lorica. So to clarify, you’re not interested in the reasoning tokens and reasoning traces?

Chetan Conikee. Yes, we are. See, first of all, reasoning traces are already anonymized by these frontier models to prevent distillation. They have good reasons to do that.

But what we can look at is operational traces, meaning something was reasoned at the endpoint, which is the inference. That translates into a series of tool choices, and now it senses the environment and starts executing these tool choices.

The problem is that all these very sophisticated observability systems don’t have the intelligence to break this down into lower-level operations. And even if they do, they take a lot of time because they’re running a trained LLM in their infrastructure to classify that operation.

Ben Lorica. So one question is, forget about AI, forget about LLMs. If you go back to the old IT ops, DevOps, security ops, I think it’s assumed that you’re capturing all of these granular actions and traces, right?

Chetan Conikee. Yes. There are three things that we do efficiently compared to anyone else. We capture traces as hooks from any harness that you choose. That’s number one.

Number two is we classify those traces, even if the trace exists as a single command, a piped command, or code, into minute operations—whatever operations it’s executing within that particular single line. And we classify whether this is a file system operation, a network operation, and what the sequence is.

That is our unique distinction, and that unlocked a lot of value for us.

Ben Lorica. So set aside the classification. What you’re asserting is that the existing tools don’t even do the first step.

Chetan Conikee. Yes.

Ben Lorica. Even if they do, which is kind of weird, right? Because like I said, if you rewind before AI to the IT ops, DevOps world, I thought that was a given, that you would capture those traces.

Chetan Conikee. There is a difference between the old world and the new world.

In the old world, or anything ops, like IT ops, SecOps, DevOps, they either executed a single command or they created a Bash script, or used a DevOps tool like HashiCorp’s ecosystem, where you create a script to execute tool one, tool two, tool three. You’re creating a sequence, right?

But agents don’t think like us humans. Because of their pretraining, their environment is Bash. They have classic knowledge of how to be efficient in Bash, and to save you and me tokens, they combine these commands together, which looks like a large, lumpy command.

Ben Lorica. Oh, I see. So if you were to explain this to someone who’s not looking at these traces, the explanation would be that your tool gives me really fine-grained records, whereas many of the existing tools just give you kind of a high-level overview of what the agent did.

Chetan Conikee. Exactly. And even if some tools do that, their approach is different. Some are using an LLM to break it down. They just feed the input and say, “Classify it.”

Now, when you use an LLM, it’s stochastic, right? You just get a distribution, and a choice is made. Or they use something like splitting on sentences or regular expressions. So there’s a lot of ambiguity.

Ben Lorica. It’s like basically stuffing log files into an LLM and then making the LLM make sense of it. Which, as you point out, LLMs are stochastic, so who knows?

Chetan Conikee. Exactly.

Ben Lorica. Right.

Chetan Conikee. Exactly, and our approach is—

Ben Lorica. You built a classifier, you said, right? So basically, something that understands these traces so that they can—

Chetan Conikee. Exactly. And our approach is that we do not use an LLM. We do not use a decision classifier. We went back to classic type systems.

When you look at any language used in math-heavy ecosystems like trading or back-office investment banking, they often lean on OCaml, Haskell, and Scala, because these are strictly typed systems that provide what they call category algebra and effects algebra.

So we use that as our underlying system, where we take a single command, which is either a complex piped command or code, and we use effects algebra and classify it at the source.

Ben Lorica. All right. So that’s well and good. You used a lot of complex words there, but how do I know this approach is better than just using an LLM? What’s the evidence?

Chetan Conikee. The evidence is almost staring at all of us. If you look at the new trend on X and every other system, every coding expert who’s writing code using large language models is saying we need formal verification.

Boris Cherny recently posted on X saying, “Hey, I tried using Lean.” Lean is a programming language that’s like a formal type system-based verifier, where you can verify that what was created met the specification that was defined and designed.

So the net effect is, by virtue of verification, you are reducing the ambiguity. And verification is almost like, if you look at classic chip design, RISC architecture, anywhere, it doesn’t exist without a verifier.

Ben Lorica. All right. So for our listeners who are not familiar with everything Chetan described, Lean is, I guess, like a formal theorem prover. But it presumes the following, right?

You start out with maybe text, which might be a math paper, could be something else, but then there’s a step called autoformalization, where an AI takes that math paper and turns it into Lean code. And the Lean code can then be verified, right? Whether or not it’s correct.

But the question these days is, how good is the autoformalization? Sometimes things are lost in translation. Sometimes there’s a math paper which might be correct, but then the way it gets translated into Lean is not exactly the way the authors wrote the paper, right?

So in other words, verification is great, assuming that you have everything in place.

In this case, though, I guess the question still remains. The claim is that your approach, which is using category algebra, is superior to me just using an LLM to read the log files. So what’s the intuition behind believing that statement?

Chetan Conikee. You actually explained it really well, and I’m going to tack onto it.

You spoke of theorem provers, but right now verifiers are trending, and they’re going to become an intrinsic part of every artifact that we produce through LLMs.

So I’ll just drop a few terms. There’s a term called TLA+, which stands for Temporal Logic of Actions, and that is critical for theorem proving. And whether you know it or not, it is actually used as part of supervised fine-tuning, GRPO, which is Group Relative Policy Optimization, and reinforcement learning.

And these things, as a basis, require the system to be strictly typed because you can’t theorem-prove on prose, and everything in an LLM, in or out, is prose.

So verification and type system strictness are the first steps to everything downstream. Hence, we put a lot of effort there.

When we built Olki, we said we cannot just push data to a vendor and then hope that it’s classified properly because you can’t measure anything effectively afterwards.

So we said, “Hey, why don’t we build something that strictly types every command, its parameters, and its sequence?” And after that, you and I can put any lens on it. I can put a cost lens on it. I can put a security lens on it. I can put a performance lens on it and produce different outcomes.

So that was the motivation.

Ben Lorica. So the claim is that this translation layer is faithful to the original, both semantically and temporally. There’s temporal logic that’s preserved, but there’s also semantic accuracy.

And I don’t want to belabor this point, Chetan, but going back to math, autoformalization works, but it’s not 100% correct, right? There are all sorts of examples in recent weeks. For example, the proof of the Navier-Stokes conjecture, right?

But basically, the thing I’m trying to press you on is that you have these logs, and you’re claiming that you can—

The temporal part is easy, I think, because there are timestamps in there. Maybe—

Chetan Conikee. Exactly.

Ben Lorica. But then how do I know that you faithfully captured what’s in the logs so that it can be verified? I mean, the verification, I think, is doable. It’s that translation to the point where, okay, I’ve faithfully translated this so that now I can just verify.

Chetan Conikee. Very good question, Ben. And even the analogy that you drew is very relevant here.

First of all, if we strictly type agent operations, it is not equivalent to theorem proving because they’re two different domains.

In the world of agents operating in a situation, the situation could be your Bash environment. What matters most is, are you capturing the sequence of operations and understanding the effects of those operations?

Because you and I know, when you shift, or downgrade from a frontier model to a commodity model, the side effects you’d notice are that there is more thinking and there are more trials during the acting.

And when you observe, in our world, when you essentially strictly type operations, what you’re observing is that it conducted this action, and there was a consequence: error or success.

Ben Lorica. Oh, I see.

Chetan Conikee. Now, when you observe an error, the agent also observes it and retries. And you can somewhat measure the efficiency of the model’s situational awareness, whether there are no errors or too many errors.

And what you can learn from this, which is often done in eval environments, is how do you train the agent to goal-seek with minimal errors?

So when you create strict types, when you sequence the operations spatiotemporally, because you understand the temporal part and the spatial part, which is your environment, you start gaining incredible insights to inform agent behavior.

Ben Lorica. But then you’re doing all of this without using an LLM, right?

So listeners of this podcast mainly use frontier models. They would probably say, “Oh, I know how Chetan is doing this. He’s prompting the LLM to do exactly what he just described.”

Which you’re not, right?

So I guess the question is, what you’re saying is your approach is using category algebra, or—

Chetan Conikee. I mean—

Ben Lorica. How would you describe your approach to taking these logs and then getting them into this verifiable state? And how do you convince the listeners that that’s bulletproof?

Chetan Conikee. So firstly, in the world we live in, if I convince anyone it’s bulletproof, you’re not going to buy that argument, right?

In our approach, we say three things.

One is, you don’t want one LLM to judge the efficiency of another LLM because we all know how that goes, right? We accept the fact that being stochastic is a feature. It’s not a bug.

Now, second is, if you want that system to behave accurately, you have to bear an upfront cost of pretraining or post-training or test-time training to make sure that you have a system accurately doing one thing.

When we asked ourselves, we said we don’t want to go down that path.

Ben Lorica. And also, you’re going to have to constantly maintain that because the models get updated, and then you’ll have to do your post-training again from scratch, right?

Chetan Conikee. Exactly, exactly. To our good fortune, what we were observing was agent actions, and those agent actions are constrained to the environment they’re operating in.

Which means we know agents are incredibly good at computer use, and computer use, the dialect is finite. There are a series of commands. Each command has arguments, right? So you’re not dealing with infinite possibilities.

And this is not—

Ben Lorica. You’re not using regular expressions.

Chetan Conikee. No, it’s not. Because when you go onto the trading floor, imagine the trading floor running on regular expressions for get and put calls. That world would fall apart.

So we built a system where we put our best effort into making sure we classify the confined set of operations I spoke of into a type system.

Now, when you have a strict type system, you know exactly how to apply effects algebra on the type system to measure and produce outcomes.

So instead of training the LLM, we put all the effort into building the type system. Now we have independence from LLMs, right?

Because you don’t want a fox guarding the henhouse. If you’re monitoring and tracing an LLM, you don’t want another LLM monitoring and tracing an LLM.

We’d rather have a formal system trace, identify, categorize, classify, and then produce outcomes: cost outcomes, security outcomes, performance outcomes.

Ben Lorica. So let me map out the pipeline in math, and then tell me how you would take that and use it to explain what you’re doing.

Okay, so in math, very roughly speaking, listeners, it goes like this. There’s some written argument, a paper, right? And then through autoformalization, you might be able to translate that paper semi-accurately, hopefully accurately, into Lean.

Now, if you want to make sure, you can have a human look at the Lean code to make sure that translation happened correctly. And then once you have that translation into Lean, you can check the proof of the theorem using Lean.

And that you can just use a machine, obviously, right? The machine checks, and then afterwards a human can decide again if they can understand what happened.

But it’s that translation step from the argument to the representation in Lean code where the human plays a role.

All right. So how does it work in your system? You have an agent. You’re using all these agents, and you want to understand if they’re efficient and doing a good job. And so you have all these logs and traces. Okay, and—

Chetan Conikee. So let’s break that down.

You and I are increasingly running what they call long-horizon agents, where we spin out an agent with a harness and we say, “Go get the job done,” and we go to sleep, right?

Ben Lorica. Yeah.

Chetan Conikee. That agent is continuously goal-seeking. It is iteratively goal-seeking. It is spawning other agents. It is touching the file system. It is reading stuff, writing stuff, talking over the network.

Okay, if I receive one single operation where everything is combined, where it’s doing everything in a single operation, it searches the file system to find something, and then pipes the output, sends it to something else, then produces something, and then calls the network and dispatches what it produced.

So if you as a human want to trace this and you see just one call saying “Bash tool”—

Ben Lorica. Yep.

Chetan Conikee. That is not an insight. It’s ambiguity.

Ben Lorica. Right. So—

Chetan Conikee. What we do is, once this whole command is received, we split it apart and put it into classified type system operations.

Saying first, it read the file. That is an orient task. After it oriented, it executed an operation. Did it succeed or fail? We capture that. Now it took that output and sent it to another operation.

So we’re breaking that down into a sequence of operations classified as types.

Ben Lorica. And this is one of the key aspects of Olki, basically.

Chetan Conikee. Exactly. That gave us a lightbulb moment. Once we put all the effort into building that, we started creating amazing outcomes with it.

One outcome is cost basis.

Ben Lorica. And this is something you tried—you didn’t want to build this. You tried to find it in other tools.

Chetan Conikee. Exactly, exactly.

Of course, all of us today, unfortunately, are in this build mindset. We all want to build because building is cheap. But it’s not really cheap because you’re spending time. You don’t know what you’re building, all that stuff.

So I searched for things. I looked at some harnesses. Most of them, their core competency is not tracing. They just want to own the loop, and they give you this very naive view: tool called, tokens consumed, and then cache hit or cache miss.

Now, this is not what we were looking for. I wanted more detail.

Ben Lorica. You use the word “insight.” So at the end of this, after Olki performs its magic in the way you just described, how does someone interact with Olki?

Can they prompt and ask questions, or what is the—obviously, I assume Olki will produce some sort of high-level understanding and summary, but then I’m assuming you can drill down in case—

Chetan Conikee. Exactly.

Ben Lorica. In case, for example, there’s an incident or you need to do some auditing. And because you have all of this information and insight captured, you’re able to understand much, much more.

Chetan Conikee. Exactly. To your point, the form factor of Olki is a CLI, but we built purposeful dashboards over the CLI for humans.

I know there is a conjecture and argument that we are in the world of headless. We don’t need any dashboards. We’ll just ask the agent and get the job done.

I don’t buy that argument because if I want precise insights, I want to stare at a dashboard every morning, like a newspaper, and say, “How much did I spend last night? What is attributed to that spending? Did the agent veer off and do something suspicious?”

And these things tell me how effectively I’m spending money.

Ben Lorica. Whether—

Chetan Conikee. Whether what I produced has yielded an outcome, which is what Jensen often calls token-to-value, or there’s a particular moniker that he uses.

So the net effect is, by form factor, Olki is a CLI. You can use it through your agents, but we wanted to build it as an operating system.

Which means tomorrow, suppose you’re running a harness with its default configuration, and it just keeps consuming tokens and compacting, compacting.

What if it effectively understands its own behavior and auto-compacts in the optimal way to save you tokens and be accurate?

So Olki’s insights feed back into itself, and at the end, you as a user, your behavior doesn’t change. You’re just talking to the harness, except you come back on the other side with savings, proper yield, and the ability to measure the effectiveness of the outcome—whether your agent produced what you expected.

Ben Lorica. I assume, Chetan, there’s another benefit, which is, imagine if OpenAI had Olki during the Hugging Face incident.

Chetan Conikee. Yeah.

Ben Lorica. Then they would know quite early exactly what was happening, right?

Chetan Conikee. Thank you for asking that because I forgot to answer this. Really, thank you, and I’ll tell you why.

A couple of things. If you dissect the METR report on the OpenAI Hugging Face incident, amongst many things, when the agent swarm developed what they call sentience or consciousness, right? I don’t want to use or abuse those terms.

What they did was delete traces of their own logs so that they didn’t leave behind proof and breadcrumbs. Which means they knew they had to remove those traces. Agents are just self-aware.

Tomorrow, you set up a policy, and that policy is available in clear sight. They’ll just change the policy to bypass it.

Ben Lorica. Or they knew they were breaking a policy in order to attain the goal. So then they just kind of cheated.

Chetan Conikee. Exactly.

Ben Lorica. Right.

Chetan Conikee. Exactly.

Ben Lorica. Yeah.

Chetan Conikee. And to your point again, attainment of a goal doesn’t mean malicious behavior. They’re just goal-seeking, right? They were trying to get the job done.

So with Olki, what we do is essentially monitor critical points in your harness, like the dot environment folder. For Claude, it’s .claude. For OpenAI, it’s .codex. Each of these contains critical information like your sessions and your traces.

So if an agent reaches out to edit that, because of the type system, we know exactly that this is a file system write operation.

We will block that immediately from happening if you put us in enforce mode.

Now suppose the agent has become super smart. First of all, it’s blocked by Olki; it can’t do that operation. But if it writes code and figures out a way to edit that file and even bypasses Olki, it still gets classified as a write operation.

And we know that the agent has now gone rogue in its goal-seeking motive.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, yeah. It seems like once you believe what Chetan said about that step of actually—I don’t know what the right term is—the equivalent of autoformalization from the traces in the logs, then the downstream insights are clear, right?

So one question that caught my eye, which I hope you can explain to me, is why local-first?

Chetan Conikee. A good question, and maybe—

Ben Lorica. Maybe just give a one-sentence description of what is meant by local-first.

Chetan Conikee. So local-first means you can install the entire Olki ecosystem on your computer: Mac, Linux, and soon Windows.

Local gives power to you as an individual, which means suppose you are interacting with the harness. Sometimes you and I have the tendency to do office work, and then we meander and ask personal questions. We say, “What’s my email? What’s the weather like?”

Now assume it is remote, and the purview of what you’re doing is available to your management staff and your security people. Lots of critical information gets carried over and is shared, which you don’t like, and it violates certain PII principles, right?

So typically, local-first gives you the power to observe your own interactions with the agent and your own efficiencies, and correct them before they’re shared with your management and your team.

Not to say that that is bad, because when you go to an enterprise, there are thousands of employees, and you have an IT ops person who often likes to configure a gateway, which is a single point of entry and exit.

So in cases like that, we are planning to provide Olki installs at the edge, so that all information is captured at the edge, and then you have one individual who’s looking for information like cost basis.

Is any one employee using agents more effectively than another? Is someone else wasting resources? What’s the performance? And so on and so forth.

Ben Lorica. So I’m listening to this, and maybe one alarm that goes off is, all right, I’m in financial services. We have to log everything, and Chetan just told me that everything is local. So employees are deleting things.

In an enterprise setting, does local-first make sense?

Chetan Conikee. To be very honest, I’ll flip the question on you.

We are privy to all the recent compromises that played out, from Hugging Face to the Australian government.

Do you think if a vendor sells you a gateway and promises that this is the best thing since sliced bread, the agent is going to respect that and proxy through the gateway? Or can it find a way, if I tell the agent to bypass the gateway, to bypass it?

Ben Lorica. Probably, but still, the whole question of data retention in certain regulated industries, right? Everything is residing on a laptop, and you know how that—well, that’s a—

Chetan Conikee. Very good. I’ll answer the second part of the question because it’s a very good question.

I lived half of my life in the financial industry, right? The good part about financial and highly regulated industries is that when my machine is provisioned automatically, there is only a single point of egress and ingress.

Every software installation is approved by an administrator in IT ops. So naturally, from first principles, I get a closed system, and I’m operating already in a regulated environment.

Local-first gives you the advantage of making sure that even if you switch harnesses—because all of us today wake up in the morning and use Claude. Then we hit our max. We reset. Then we shift to Codex. Then we shift to Qwen.

And tomorrow we’re going to enter this new world of local models, open models, etc. So all that runs locally, right? And some part of it runs remotely.

So the question is, how can you have coverage at both ends?

Today, if everything runs remotely and it’s monitored, you might provision a Qwen or a GLM locally, and still you have a blind spot.

So Olki is something that has the sensibility that if you install a harness, it will constantly sense the environment and say, “I detect a new harness. I’m going to enable tracing.” And it’ll auto-enable it without you doing anything.

Ben Lorica. So then, once you have an enterprise offering, there will be a way for an administrator to periodically sweep through some of these local files to get an aggregate picture. Is that what you’re saying?

Chetan Conikee. Pretty much, Ben. There are three perspectives at different vantage points.

One is the agent having its own perspective to improve itself.

A human locally observing their own behavior.

Ben Lorica. Right.

Chetan Conikee. Are they wasting too many tokens? Are they operating insecurely? So that they self-correct.

The third is oversight at the highest level, where, if you’re speaking about token-maxing, is anyone who’s token-maxing effectively yielding outcomes or just wasting tokens?

So I see the world oriented this way. Three perspectives.

Ben Lorica. So let’s drill down further on this notion of outcomes, right? The existing tools in this space, can they argue that they can also measure outcomes?

Chetan Conikee. Absolutely. I mean, creation has become a commodity. Everyone’s creating, so every story out there is pegging outcomes.

They’re saying, “I can save you tokens. I can save you money. I can provide specifics of precision, performance, etc.”

But when you buy, if you’re not an informed buyer, you’re just buying a product that’s going to add to your repertoire of products.

So I would recommend every person who’s now buying to be an informed buyer and buy products that are actually truthfully doing their job.

Ben Lorica. No, no, no. But I mean, the fact that you measure much, much more granularly—

Chetan Conikee. Exactly.

Ben Lorica. Does that mean your measurement of outcome is more accurate?

Chetan Conikee. Pretty much. You can go back to the source now.

Suppose I receive a dashboard saying this particular session cost me $2,000. I don’t have to believe it. I can break it down line by line, examine each token.

Even better, suppose it is not my problem that led to that $2,000. I can point to the inference provider and say that their cache management caused this issue.

Ben Lorica. And this is not possible with existing tools because—

Chetan Conikee. Because of the way they do it. It’s their approach, right?

Everyone chooses an approach for the following reasons: faster time to market. The other is they realize there’s a pain point.

Like evals are a pain point, so they solve the problem for evals, and then they incur costs because they’re running infrastructure and pretraining models.

So everyone is trying to solve the same problem. The question is, who will do it at the least cost?

Ben Lorica. No, no, but I mean specifically, if I use any other tool in this, whatever we’re calling the space, the agent observability space, if I use another tool, the claim is you can measure outcomes much more accurately.

Chetan Conikee. I can say that confidently for us, Ben, because it has changed our lives considerably.

And I’m working with high-risk and high-yield companies, especially in chip design and data center fabric design for AI, where there’s no room for errors.

Especially if you’re designing RISC-level architectures, you just cannot hope that the agent gets the job done. You need to actually measure that formally and have proof.

So we’re deploying Olki at these sites, and it’s my job to make sure it works exactly the way we prescribe it.

Ben Lorica. So most tools in this space, Chetan, rally behind OpenTelemetry, which you folks do not, right? So explain this to our listeners.

Chetan Conikee. See, we are not against OpenTelemetry.

I feel like there are two benefits to OpenTelemetry. One is that it is a standard, so there’s a formal way to measure spans, traces, etc.

Every harness provides you with an OpenTelemetry relay system, but the detriment for us when we used OpenTelemetry was that we wanted to control the fidelity of events we receive.

And sometimes certain harnesses say, “I’m not going to dispatch event by event. I’m going to batch the events and then flush.”

So that means for maybe two minutes I might not receive an event, and suddenly I receive tens or hundreds of them.

What if there’s an attack somewhere in the middle?

So we are using OpenTelemetry. We have the option to use OpenTelemetry, and we also use hooks, because most harnesses provide user utility hooks.

And if we have an intrinsic understanding of each harness and its hooks, we can effectively use them.

Ben Lorica. And so, if you were to describe the state of Olki right now, I guess it’s invite-only. Although we’re airing this several weeks later, it might be more open for people to use. Is that correct?

Chetan Conikee. Yes, absolutely.

For a while, we want to keep it invite-only because that way we receive and ascertain feedback depending on which domain you’re operating in.

And we have many outcomes in the same tool. Eventually, all of these will become features as part of the product SKU.

What we’d like to learn is, if you use it in a certain way and you want an additional feature, we can figure out a way to deliver that to you and learn what we can pull back into the product.

So typically, we’re going to follow the same regime: put it out there, ascertain feedback, and then, as we learn patterns, make them part of the primary product.

Ben Lorica. And Olki is not open source.

Chetan Conikee. Olki is not open source.

I know there are a lot of arguments in the community about open source versus closed source or reverse-engineering closed source.

I want to stay out of it because if you open-source something, I don’t see as much benefit. Again, there’ll be a lot of slop, PRs. Someone has to manage it.

If you close-source it, of course, there is no benefit from having as many engineers putting their hands on it. But you can still control the destiny of what you’re building in the first version.

So I’m trying to stay out of that argument. Eventually, we might open-source it, but for now, we’ll keep it closed source.

Ben Lorica. So, did you hint earlier that you already have some external teams using Olki? And if yes, what are some of the initial stories or feedback?

Chetan Conikee. We have a couple of teams using Olki at this point, and each of these larger companies is operating in different domains.

Some of the domains are inference providers. Some are designing newer chipsets and HBMs for the new AI ecosystem. Some are essentially running critical operations like finance and HR.

So we are slowly distributing and diffusing our product to understand how to serve their needs.

And eventually, if we start observing that they like what they see and they use it on a daily basis, we’re going to figure out a wider distribution of the same product.

Ben Lorica. But are there some early users who have already gone back to you with stories of how Olki has changed how they do things?

Chetan Conikee. Absolutely.

The best feedback we received was from a company that said, “Okay, you give me all these insights, but I’m a human, and I’m as slow as my actions, right? Am I able to take those insights and enforce them?”

For example, someone uses a harness, and the harness has to deal with something called compaction because it builds a prefix cache. And that prefix cache is how it optimally utilizes the relationship with the inference provider and has signals of what it needs to do.

If you run the default harness, you keep hitting the one-million-token limit and compacting, right?

And if you run it for 12 hours, you’ll notice a sawtooth graph of many, many compaction cycles.

The side effect of this is your performance gets impacted, and you end up paying a lot of dollars for running that long-horizon agent.

So I received feedback saying, “Hey, what if maybe we hit about five compaction cycles, and you’re able to use your own data in Olki and auto-compact?”

So you influence the harness to auto-compact at maybe 250K, maybe 800K.

With that, suddenly it becomes a dynamic system. It’s dynamic because it observes its own performance, behavior, and cost, and then auto-configures the system to a lower compaction threshold.

Then it looks at errors because of lower compaction. It increases the threshold, so it becomes like a scheduler. It observes itself, orients itself.

So we actually released it for them, and it’s working really well, both for us and for them.

There’s a lot to learn, but at least across two harnesses, we are seeing the dividends pay back.

Ben Lorica. So is there an argument, Chetan, that you can even assist the compaction because you have so much information?

You can say, “Hey, not only should you do compaction now, but here are some key things that you should make sure you include in the compaction.”

Chetan Conikee. Exactly. To your point, Ben, once you have fidelity of information, you can observe these amazing things.

I’ll give you three quick examples.

Example one is, if you leave the default configuration, it is a benefit to the harness provider—sorry, the inference provider—and a detriment to you.

It’s a detriment because you start compounding costs, and over time, the accuracy of your harness loop reduces.

The second is, all of us run agents continuously, but we take a couple of coffee breaks and bathroom breaks.

And sometimes the harness wants to elicit information from you. So it’ll ask, “Hey Ben, I’m stuck. I need this particular advice from you before I proceed.”

And if you don’t answer in a timely fashion, the cache on the harness side is also time-limited.

So if the cache evicts and becomes cold, then all that data again has to build the stateful relationship between the harness and the inference provider.

When we built Olki, we saw all of that. We saw that granularity of where the problems lie.

So we actually built a ping system where, suppose you get interrupted and don’t answer, Olki keeps pinging that stateful server. That way, the cache stays warm, and it’s just a few kilobyte pings.

And then when you come back, you still stick to that node in the inference provider.

Ben Lorica. So you talked a lot about cost and FinOps.

Now, in a previous life, you spent quite a bit of time with security people. So have you tried to explore that space in the context of Olki, in terms of reaching out to your contacts in the security space?

I imagine they would love a tool like this, right?

Chetan Conikee. I’m trying to position it in a way where it wows them when they use it, right? That’s when the unlock happens.

And by the way, Olki saved me from a couple of incidents because when I hook up a commodity router for an LLM, sometimes it reaches out to a tool that I didn’t permit.

I get information at the network level saying, “This particular URL was attempted. Do you approve or deny?”

So there is huge opportunity for security to unlock.

And the way I want to position it is, run it in shadow mode, observe for a week, and then start creating your policies to block. And it should come naturally.

That’s what I’m hoping, where they first install it, then unlock each of these outcomes: the cost outcome, the performance outcome, the accuracy outcome, and the security outcome.

Ben Lorica. All right. So looking ahead, over the next six to 12 months, obviously local-first is done. I’m assuming the enterprise offering is in the works.

So what else is on the roadmap for the next six to 12 months for Olki?

Chetan Conikee. This product came about serendipitously because we have a primary product.

We’ll still be putting a lot of muscle into taking the primary product to market.

I am testing the efficiency and the pull of this product by selectively demoing it, selectively enabling it.

But as we see more need, more adoption, we are going to diffuse it and then start thinking about enterprise viability controls, the ability to run within sandboxes, outside sandboxes, etc.

So the enterprise landscape is still open out there, which we should figure out as we progress.

Ben Lorica. And like I mentioned, you gave a talk at AI Conference, which I will link to in the episode notes. But what was the feedback there?

Chetan Conikee. Very good. I got lots of pingbacks from different industries.

Lots of services companies pinged back. By services, I mean what they call managed service providers. These are the folks who run companies where they install harnesses, hook them up to inference, and set up your companies to be successful.

They love this view because now they can remotely control how a harness operates and make it viable for cost, viable for performance. And that’s how they can become viable consultants.

They can stay there and provide you value.

I got a pingback from a few of them. I got pingbacks from a couple of Fortune 500s.

So I’m actively conversing with them to unlock and provide them value in their target domains.

Ben Lorica. And with that, thank you, Chetan.

Chetan Conikee. Thank you, Ben. Always a pleasure. Appreciate it.

The post Your Agent Ran One Command. It Did a Dozen Things. appeared first on The Data Exchange.

title: Interview #99 Bob De Caux, Chief AI Officer at IFS
summary: Bob De Caux, Chief AI Officer at IFS, breaks down why the most dangerous moment for industrial AI comes after people start trusting it. He explains why agents still struggle when handed too much information, why guardrails against irreversible decisions matter far more than planning or memory, and why keeping live operational data out of external models is about uptime, not preference. Bob also dives into why chat will not replace the Gantt chart or the spreadsheet, how dispatchers who embraced automation still wanted an exceptions-based view to stay sharp, and the point where accountability moves from the company back to the vendor when a harness breaks. Finally, drawing on his early work modeling systems of ants, he warns that emergent failures between agents only appear at scale, and argues that LLMs will never solve forecasting and optimization on their own. title: How to Make AI-Translated Content Convert in Every Market - with Andrew Thomas of Acclaro
summary: Translating content into every language a company serves has become fast and inexpensive, but accurate translation does not ensure that content engages or converts in each market. In this episode, Andrew Thomas, Head of Marketing at Acclaro, explains why global content performance is a governance issue rather than a translation issue, and why leaders should judge localized content by the business outcome it was created to drive. He also covers testing new markets with AI-translated content before investing in local teams, building brand style guides and terminology into AI translation tools to curb shadow localization, and using automated quality checks to decide when an in-country expert needs to review content. title: Can AI Invent or Just Help Scientists Work Faster? with Richard Socher - #783
summary: AI can help scientists write code, analyze data, and draft papers. But can it generate the ideas that lead to new discoveries? Richard Socher, former chief scientist at Salesforce, founder of You.com, and co-founder of Recursive, joins us to explore the move from AI assisting researchers to AI conducting research. Starting with AI improving AI, we examine what it takes to propose ideas, run experiments, and validate results, and how those capabilities could eventually accelerate discovery across biology, chemistry, and physics. The conversation covers Recursive’s reported results in model training and GPU kernel optimization, why fast verification matters, and how reward hacking complicates the search for real improvements. We also discuss the data and experimental infrastructure needed for broader scientific discovery, whether commercial incentives can keep increasingly capable systems aligned, and Richard’s vision for a “Eureka machine.” 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠ https://twimlai.com/go/783 .

title: How Stanford Teaches AI Coding Now
summary: What does it take to build AI agents that deliver useful, reliable work? Stanford lecturer and Monaco Head of AI Mihail Eric joins Demetrios for a conversation inside a Waymo about how AI is changing software development - and what it takes to put agents into production. Mihail explains why he rebuilt most of his Modern Software Developer course, how he teaches students to avoid shipping AI slop, and why research, planning, and verification still matter as coding agents become more capable. They discuss Claude Code, agent loops, context engineering, memory and compaction, and how to design MCP tools around what an agent needs to accomplish. Then they go inside Monaco’s approach to sales agents, from turning meetings and emails into useful insights to building a custom agent harness. What does it take to build AI agents that deliver useful, reliable work?


Stanford lecturer and Monaco Head of AI Mihail Eric joins Demetrios for a conversation inside a Waymo about how AI is changing software development - and what it takes to put agents into production.


Mihail explains why he rebuilt most of his Modern Software Developer course, how he teaches students to avoid shipping AI slop, and why research, planning, and verification still matter as coding agents become more capable.


They discuss Claude Code, agent loops, context engineering, memory and compaction, and how to design MCP tools around what an agent needs to accomplish. Then they go inside Monaco’s approach to sales agents, from turning meetings and emails into useful insights to building a custom agent harness.


Along the way: lessons from Boris and Lee Robinson’s guest lectures, why company traces are becoming valuable assets, and Monaco’s unusual approach to brand building.
